clue.text: Outlaw the war-plane, some said

explanation.surface: An order to ban an aircraft, as some people put it.
explanation.walkthrough: In wartime RAF slang an enemy aircraft was called a bandit, hence 'some said'.
explanation.definitionFit: A brigand living outside the law is the first sense; the second is airmen's slang for a hostile fighter plane.

clue.text: Solitary drinker's order on entering

indicators.note: entering says the word on goes inside the drink ordered

parts.note: a drinker in a pub might order ale
taken as written

explanation.surface: A lone drinker orders a pint on coming into the bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drinker's order' sounds like a request; it is just the drink ordered in a pub.
explanation.definitionFit: Solitary and on one's own are synonyms, both meaning unaccompanied.

clue.text: Assume in proof of title its laid down

indicators.note: in says the word for assume sits inside the document proving ownership

parts.note: a deed is the legal document that proves ownership of property
to posit is to assume something as a basis for argument

explanation.surface: A legal phrase about presuming title is established in a document.
explanation.walkthrough: 'its' is a link word, probably 'it's' in the original printing; the surface hides a legal phrase about establishing title.
explanation.definitionFit: Something put down or placed somewhere has been laid down, as a sediment or a sum in a bank.

clue.text: Mark and Jack become united

indicators.note: united says the two words are joined side by side to form one

parts.note: a jack tar is an old name for a sailor, so jack can mean tar
to get can mean to become, as in get angry

explanation.surface: Two men called Mark and Jack join forces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark' and 'Jack' look like two names; Mark is the definition, Jack gives TAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A mark is something aimed at, a bullseye or goal, the same as a target.

clue.text: Game in which we should keep cool

definitions.text: in which we should keep cool

explanation.surface: A game played somewhere chilly.
explanation.walkthrough: The game is the British name for checkers; draughts are also currents of cool air.
explanation.definitionFit: The board game known in America as checkers is one sense; the other is breezes of cold air that keep a room cool.

clue.text: Perhaps refugee spends QUO. Roe paid out

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Perhaps refugee spends QUO. Roe paid out': SPENDS + ROE PAID leaves CL for the anagram, and 'QUO' is an OCR garble no search restored.
annotationWithheld.clue: Perhaps refugee spends QUO. Roe paid out

clue.text: Unusual for girl student after taking up degree

indicators.note: after says the girl and student come behind the degree
in a down clue taking up means the degree is read upwards

parts.note: BA is a Bachelor of Arts degree
Norma is a girl's name
L is a learner, the student driver's plate

explanation.surface: A girl student does something odd after taking up a degree course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking up' turns BA into AB, which comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: Something out of the ordinary deviates from the norm, so both mean irregular.

clue.text: Fee in US for playing piano?

explanation.surface: A question about what an American pianist charges.
explanation.walkthrough: In US slang a grand is a thousand dollars; a grand is also the large concert piano.
explanation.definitionFit: A thousand dollars is a sizeable fee in American slang, and the big concert piano is one played in performance.

clue.text: Bell desirable on one such vehicle

definitions.text: Bell desirable on one such vehicle

parts.words: Bell desirable on one such vehicle
parts.note: alludes to the song Daisy Bell, about a bicycle built for two, where Daisy is the desired one

explanation.surface: A remark that a cycle bell would be useful on this type of vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: Bell is Daisy Bell of the old music-hall song, whose suitor offers a bicycle built for two.
explanation.definitionFit: A tandem or small car with room for a pair of riders is the vehicle in the song.

clue.text: Dogberry's "odorous" simile

parts.note: Dogberry, the bungling constable in Much Ado About Nothing, says such likenings are odorous, mangling odious

explanation.surface: A Shakespearean constable's smelly figure of speech.
explanation.walkthrough: Dogberry's malapropism turns the proverb that likenings are odious into 'odorous'.
explanation.definitionFit: A simile likens one thing to another, so it is a kind of likening of two things.

clue.text: Prophet in Greek island got beheaded

indicators.note: beheaded says the island loses its first letter

parts.note: Samos is an island in the eastern Aegean

explanation.surface: A biblical prophet on a Greek island lost his head.
explanation.definitionFit: One of the minor Old Testament seers has a book of the Bible in his name.

clue.text: Message from poor sailor found on shore?

definitions.text: Message from poor sailor found on shore?

parts.words: Message from poor sailor found on shore?
parts.note: a seasick sailor's complaint would be that the ocean is hell, and the item lies on the beach

explanation.surface: A note from a wretched sailor washed up on the beach.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as SEA'S HELL it is the miserable sailor's message.
explanation.definitionFit: The empty casing of a mollusc washed up on a beach is what one finds on the shore.

clue.text: Stern director

parts.note: reads as a strict boss, but stern is the back of a boat and the steering blade sits there

explanation.surface: A strict boss.
explanation.definitionFit: The blade at a vessel's back end steers its course.

clue.text: Mark's place, perhaps

explanation.surface: A man's home, maybe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark's' looks like a man's name; 's is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A stain or dot is one sense; the other is a location, as in a nice picnic site.

clue.text: Some reading about crime in the Brontes' home

indicators.note: about says the reading matter goes round the crime

parts.note: a page is a portion of a book to read
arson is the crime of setting fire to property

explanation.surface: Something to read on a crime set in the Bronte family house.
explanation.walkthrough: The Bronte sisters grew up at Haworth Parsonage in Yorkshire, where their father was clergyman.
explanation.definitionFit: The Brontes' father was perpetual curate of Haworth, so the family lived in the vicar's house.

clue.text: Fellow let us have wreaths

parts.note: a chap is a fellow, a man
let us contracts to let's

explanation.surface: A man invites us to share some garlands.
explanation.definitionFit: Garlands of flowers worn on the head are circlets or wreaths.

clue.text: Abandoned revolver, as sergeant ordered?

parts.note: something abandoned has been left
a wheel is something that revolves

explanation.surface: A gun dumped, as a sergeant instructed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolver' wants to be a pistol; it is anything that turns.
explanation.definitionFit: A drill-square command telling a marching line to pivot to port is what a sergeant shouts.

clue.text: Mexican cake's the wrong one — quite upsetting

parts.note: a tort is a civil wrong in law
I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: in a down clue upsetting turns the word for quite on its head

parts.note: all can mean quite or completely, as in all alone

explanation.surface: Getting a Mexican cake wrong is quite upsetting.
explanation.definitionFit: A thin flat round of unleavened maize bread is a staple of Mexican cooking.

clue.text: Poster in station, perhaps, seen before crossing city

parts.note: BR is British Rail, which ran the stations
a poster is an ad
a ford is a shallow river crossing

explanation.surface: An advertisement in a railway station seen before a level crossing.
explanation.walkthrough: BR is British Rail, the former national railway in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A city in West Yorkshire, England, once a wool-trade centre.

clue.text: Food from Japan or China?

parts.note: the question mark hints that the region of Japan and China, abbreviated, yields a word for meals

explanation.surface: A question about oriental cuisine.
explanation.walkthrough: Abbreviate the name of the region that holds Japan and China (the distant East) and the result is a word for food.
explanation.definitionFit: Food or diet in general, as in plain wholesome meals.

clue.text: Cricketer wanted to get at the beer

definitions.text: wanted to get at the beer

explanation.surface: A cricketer keen for a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the two batsmen who start an innings are its first pair; a bottle tool also takes the cap off.
explanation.definitionFit: A batsman who starts the innings is one sense; the other is the tool for prising caps off bottles.

clue.text: Doctor clothed Wi go out fighting?

annotationWithheld.why: Clue held as 'Doctor clothed Wi go out fighting?': MB inside COAT gives the answer, but the word for COAT is lost in the OCR garble 'Wi go out'.
annotationWithheld.clue: Doctor clothed Wi go out fighting?

clue.text: Dim king overcome by leader of barons

indicators.note: in a down clue overcome by puts the baron letter on top of the king
leader of picks the first letter of barons

parts.note: Lear is Shakespeare's tragic king

explanation.surface: A dim-witted monarch defeated by the chief of the barons.
explanation.definitionFit: Bleary eyes are dim or misty, so the word means hazy.

clue.text: Authorizes construction of: more pews

indicators.note: construction says the letters are built into a new shape

explanation.surface: A church committee authorizes building more pews.
explanation.definitionFit: To give someone power or authority to act is to authorize them.

clue.text: Anglers' requirements — some are elsewhere

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Fishing gear: some are kept somewhere else.
explanation.definitionFit: Fishermen wind their line on spools fixed to the rod.

clue.text: In a dangerous position, I take it

definitions.text: In a dangerous position, I take it

parts.words: In a dangerous position, I take it
parts.note: someone in peril takes caution, so the clue is what one takes when in danger

explanation.surface: Someone in a precarious spot assumes something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I take it' looks like 'I suppose'; read literally, the thing one takes when in danger.
explanation.definitionFit: Caution or heed is what anyone in peril exercises.

clue.text: Is beaten when carrying spirit in US city

indicators.note: carrying says the word for being beaten holds the spirit inside it

parts.note: someone who is beaten loses
an angel is a heavenly spirit

explanation.surface: Someone loses while carrying a bottle of spirits in an American city.
explanation.definitionFit: The Californian metropolis is the second largest city in the USA.

clue.text: Fruit might appear to be an apple

parts.note: a pear is a fruit
main means strength, as in might and main

explanation.surface: A fruit that may look like an apple.
explanation.definitionFit: An old English variety of eating fruit from the orchard, red-skinned and crisp.

clue.text: Enjoy "Shirley"? Not finished re-reading

indicators.note: re-reading says the shortened name is read again in a new order
not finished says the name loses its last letter

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Enjoying the novel Shirley so much one re-reads it before finishing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not finished' drops the Y; 're-reading' rearranges SHIRLE.
explanation.definitionFit: To savour or take pleasure in something is to like it greatly.
